theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A team leader has five jobs waiting. Which tool helps sort them by how urgent and how important each one is?
options: A cut list for each of the five jobs
A weld map drawn for the largest job
An urgent–important matrix
A bill of materials for the week

options: Make the stairs safe at once, then plan the repair with the supervisor
Finish the paid job first, then look at the handrail some time next week

Customers only want to deal with the team members
Important tasks are always too easy for a leader

questions.stem: Which 5S step is about written routines and checklists, so every area is kept the same way by everyone?
options: Sort

options: Tell the team to work faster so that the lost time is made up again

questions.stem: Why should team members have a say when the weekly work plan is made?
options: So the leader can blame them if the plan fails

questions.stem: A new trainee joins your team. How should their first week be organised?
options: Induction, a safety briefing, then simple tasks with a buddy
Straight onto the hardest welding job to test their skills
A week of sweeping only, with no other tasks given

options: Give it to the one who shouts the loudest

options: To give the team something to do at the end of the day

options: To set the price of a standard job when quoting for new customers
To decide who is the senior worker in the team

options: 2 days

options: To decide who will be blamed for all of the problems that came up in the week
To read out every job card from the week

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: Each person works 7.5 productive hours a day. How many productive hours do 3 people give in a 5-day week?
What is the name of the waste caused by people moving about more than they need to, such as long walks to the store?
A job is due on Friday 20 November. It needs 4 working days and cannot start before Monday 16 November. How many spare working days are there?
What name is given to the points a team writes down at the end of a job, so the next job goes better?
Which word means getting the most work done with the least waste of time, people and materials?
Grinding discs are used at 15 a day and come in boxes of 25. How many boxes are needed for 10 working days?
What is the name of the list of all the items held in the store, with their quantities?
Which word means the amount of work a team or machine can do in a set time?
What is the name for time when a machine cannot be used because it is broken or being serviced?
Overtime is paid at 1.5 times the normal rate. The normal rate is J$1 200 an hour. What is the overtime rate per hour, in J$?
What is the name of the document that lists the duties of a job role, given to each worker?

A job is 50% done after 4 days. If the rest goes at the same rate, how many more days will it take?
What is the name of the extra stock always kept in reserve so that the store does not run out if a delivery is late?
What is the name of the list that shows which team members work which days and hours?

essays.stem: Explain how a team leader decides the order of work when several jobs, a machine breakdown and a safety repair all arrive in the same week. Use the urgent–important idea.
essays.modelAnswer: I would list everything that needs doing and sort each item by how urgent it is (how soon it must be done) and how important it is (how much harm or value it carries). Anything that is both urgent and important comes first: the safety repair, because someone could be hurt, and the breakdown if it stops other work. Safety comes before money. Important jobs that are not urgent, such as a contract due in two weeks, are planned with fixed dates so they do not become emergencies. Urgent but less important tasks, such as some phone requests, can be delegated. Things that are neither urgent nor important are left until later or dropped. I would then check the order with the supervisor, especially where a customer's date will move, tell the team and the customers about the new plan, and review it each day as things change.
markingPoints: Lists all the work and judges urgency and importance
Puts safety and work-stopping problems first
Schedules important, non-urgent jobs with fixed dates
Delegates or delays less important tasks
Confirms with the supervisor, tells team and customers, reviews daily

essays.stem: Describe how you would share out the tasks of a fabrication job among a team of five with different skills, and how you would delegate and follow up.
essays.modelAnswer: First I break the job into tasks, such as marking out, cutting, fitting, welding, grinding, painting and inspection, and note any that need a qualification, such as a coded welder. I look at the skills matrix to match people to tasks, giving the qualified work to those who hold the right tickets, and pairing a newer member with an experienced one so they learn. I try to share the work fairly and keep everyone busy, checking the order of tasks so no one is waiting. When I delegate, I explain each task clearly: what is to be done, to which drawing and standard, the deadline, the safety points, and when to report back. I check they understand and have the tools and materials. During the job I check progress at agreed times, give help or feedback, and record the work. At the end I thank the team and note what could be shared better next time.
markingPoints: Breaks the job into tasks and notes those needing qualifications
Uses the skills matrix; pairs new members with experienced ones
Shares work fairly and keeps the flow going
Delegates clearly: task, standard, deadline, safety, reporting
Follows up at set times, gives feedback and reviews

essays.stem: Explain how to work out a team's capacity for a week and compare it with the work booked. Use a worked example, and say what you would do if the work is more than the capacity.
essays.modelAnswer: Capacity is the productive time the team really has. Example: a team of 4 works 8 hours a day for 5 days, which is 160 hours. Each person loses about 1.5 hours a day to set-up, cleaning, meetings and breaks, which is 4 × 1.5 × 5 = 30 hours. One person is on leave for a day, losing another 6.5 hours. So capacity is 160 − 30 − 6.5 = 123.5 hours. Next I add up the estimated hours for every booked job: say 140 hours. The work is 16.5 hours more than the capacity. Options are: agree overtime within the Centre's rules, borrow a worker from another team, move a job with a later deadline to next week after talking to the customer, or find ways to save time, such as batching cutting. I would raise this with the supervisor early and update the plan, rather than letting jobs run late.
markingPoints: Defines capacity as real productive time
Correct worked example taking off lost time and absence
Adds up booked hours and compares
Gives options: overtime, extra help, moving jobs, saving time
Raises it early with the supervisor and updates the plan

essays.stem: Describe how you would organise the layout and storage of a welding and fabrication workshop so that work flows well and safely. Refer to 5S.
essays.modelAnswer: I would set the layout so work flows in one direction: steel store, marking and cutting, fitting, welding bays, grinding and finishing, painting, then dispatch. This cuts carrying and crossing paths. Welding bays are screened and have extraction, and painting is kept well away from hot work. Gas cylinders are stored upright and chained in a ventilated area, with fuel gases apart from oxygen. Walkways are marked and kept clear. Using 5S: Sort means removing broken tools and scrap; Set in order means a marked place for every tool, such as shadow boards and labelled racks near where they are used; Shine means cleaning daily, which also shows up leaks and damage; Standardise means written routines and checklists so everyone keeps it the same way; Sustain means checks and audits so the standard does not slip. Stock of consumables is kept close to the bays, topped up from the main store.
markingPoints: One-way flow from store to dispatch
Hot work separated from painting; screens and extraction
Safe cylinder storage and clear marked walkways
Explains all five S steps with workshop examples
Consumables kept close to where they are used

essays.stem: Explain how you would control the stock of consumables (electrodes, wire, gas and discs) so that the team does not run out and does not overstock.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would find out how fast each item is used, from past records, and how long each supplier takes to deliver. For each item I would set a minimum (safety) stock and a reorder point, which is the daily use × the delivery time + the safety stock. For example, 20 discs a day × 4 days + 20 = 100 discs. When stock reaches that level, an order is placed for a set amount. I would also set a maximum, so money and space are not tied up and items such as electrodes do not age. A simple stock card or spreadsheet records what comes in and goes out, and stock is counted regularly. Items are stored correctly: electrodes dry, low-hydrogen types in an oven once opened, wire in its packing, gas cylinders secured, and old stock used first. Problems, such as late deliveries, are reported and the levels adjusted.
markingPoints: Uses records of usage and supplier delivery times
Sets safety stock and reorder point, with a correct example
Sets a maximum to avoid overstocking
Keeps stock records and counts regularly
Stores items correctly and uses first in, first out

essays.stem: Describe how you would monitor your team's work during the week, the measures you would use, and what you would do when a job falls behind.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start each day with a short briefing and a look at the job board, so everyone knows the targets. During the day I would walk round at set times to see progress, quality and safety for myself, and talk to each person. I would use simple measures: hours used against hours planned for each job, the number of jobs finished on time, rework or repair rates, and any safety incidents or near misses. These are recorded on job sheets and a weekly summary. When a job falls behind, I first find out why, for example missing material, a machine fault or a skill gap. Then I act: move people or tasks, fix the cause, arrange extra help or overtime within the rules, and if the date cannot be met, tell the supervisor and the customer early with a new date. I record what happened so it can be avoided next time.
markingPoints: Daily briefing and job board
Regular checks of progress, quality and safety
Uses measures: hours vs plan, on-time jobs, rework, incidents
Finds the cause of delays and takes action
Tells supervisor and customer early; records lessons

essays.stem: Explain how good communication helps to organise work. Cover daily briefings, job boards, handover notes, and talking with other trades and with customers.
essays.modelAnswer: A short daily briefing tells the team the day's priorities, who does what, the hazards and any changes, and gives them a chance to raise problems. A job board shows every job's stage at a glance, so people know what to do next without waiting to be told, and the leader can spot hold-ups. Handover notes between shifts or between team members pass on what has been done, what is left, any hazards and faults, so work is not repeated or done wrongly. Talking with other trades, such as electricians or painters, lets work be planned so that teams do not get in each other's way or create hazards, such as painting near hot work. Keeping customers informed about progress, changes and delays builds trust and avoids complaints. Good communication is clear, written where it matters, checked for understanding, and two-way, so problems come to light early.
markingPoints: Daily briefing: priorities, roles, hazards, changes
Job board: shows stages and hold-ups
Handover notes: work done, left, hazards
Other trades and customers: coordinating and informing
Communication is clear, recorded, checked and two-way

essays.stem: Explain how a team leader manages their own time and deals with interruptions while still supporting the team.
essays.modelAnswer: A team leader should plan each day and week, using a to-do list with priorities marked, and block out a short, fixed time for planning and paperwork, for example the first half hour of the day. Large tasks are broken into steps with dates. Interruptions are handled by asking whether the matter is urgent: if it is, deal with it; if not, note it and deal with it at a set time. Phone calls and messages can be grouped and answered together. Some tasks can be delegated to trained team members, which also builds their skills. The leader should still be easy to reach for safety problems and questions, and walk round the workshop regularly, because supporting the team is part of the job, not an interruption. At the end of the day the leader reviews the list and carries forward anything not done.
markingPoints: Daily and weekly plan with a prioritised to-do list
Fixed time set aside for planning
Sorts interruptions by urgency; groups calls and messages
Delegates suitable tasks
Stays available for safety and support; reviews the list each day

essays.stem: Describe how you would plan a new trainee's first two weeks in your team so that they work safely and become useful quickly.
essays.modelAnswer: On the first day the trainee gets an induction: a tour of the workshop, the emergency exits and first aid, the Centre's rules, PPE issue and a safety briefing on the main hazards. They meet the team and are given a buddy, an experienced member who will guide them. I would find out what they can already do and note it on the skills matrix. In the first week they do simple tasks, such as marking out, cutting and cleaning, under supervision, with clear instructions and checks. In the second week they move on to tasks such as fitting and tacking, and practise welding on test pieces before any customer work. I would check their progress each day, give feedback, and write down the training they have had. At the end of the two weeks we would agree the next targets. The trainee should feel free to ask questions at any time.
markingPoints: Induction: tour, emergency points, rules, PPE, safety briefing
Buddy assigned; skills checked and recorded
Simple supervised tasks first, building up in the second week
Daily checks, feedback and training records
Agrees next targets; encourages questions

essays.stem: Explain how a weekly review and continuous improvement can make a team's work better organised. Give two examples of improvements.
essays.modelAnswer: A short weekly review compares what was planned with what really happened: jobs finished on time, hours used, rework, safety issues and any problems with materials or machines. The team says what went well and what got in the way. The leader picks one or two problems to fix, agrees an action with a person and a date, and checks next week whether it worked. Small changes made week by week add up to a better-run workshop, and the team feels involved. Example 1: welders lost time walking to the store for discs and electrodes, so a small stock was set up at each bay and topped up daily, saving about half an hour per person per day. Example 2: jobs were held up waiting for the only plasma cutter, so a shared booking sheet was started and cutting for several jobs was batched, cutting delays.
markingPoints: Compares the plan with what happened, using measures
Team takes part; problems chosen and actions agreed with owner and date
Checks that actions worked; small steady changes
Example 1 of an improvement, clearly explained
Example 2 of an improvement, clearly explained

practical1.title: Organise a workshop bay using 5S and set up a visual job board
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the group a cluttered workshop bay or store area and a list of the jobs planned for the coming week. As a group, photograph the area 'before', then apply 5S: sort out what is not needed (tag broken tools and scrap), set the useful items in order with marked places (a shadow board drawn on board or card, labelled shelves or bins), clean the area, and write a one-page standard (checklist) for keeping it that way. Then set up a job board with 'to do', 'doing' and 'done' columns and put the week's jobs on it, with who is responsible and the due date. Each member leads one part (for example sort, set in order, shine, the standard, or the job board) and all members take part in each step. Finish with a short walk-through for the assessor explaining the changes. Photograph each stage and add the photos, the tag list and the standard to the group's practical.
materials: A cluttered bay or store area chosen by the assessor
Red tags or labels, marker pens, tape and labels
Board or heavy card for a shadow board, and hooks
Cleaning materials: brooms, brushes, rags, bins
Whiteboard or board for the job board, with cards or sticky notes
photos: Items tagged during the sort, with the tag list
The shadow board or labelled shelves
The written standard (checklist) posted in the area
The job board with the week's jobs, owners and dates
The group explaining the changes to the assessor
checklist: Led their part and took part in every step
Sorted items sensibly, tagging broken or unneeded items and recording them
Gave each kept item a clear, marked place near where it is used
Cleaned safely and reported any damage found
Helped write a clear standard that others could follow
Set up the job board with owners and due dates
Explained the changes clearly in the walk-through
safety: Wear gloves and safety boots when moving steel, tools and scrap
Lift with a straight back, and get help with heavy or awkward items
Do not use or test tagged broken tools
Keep walkways clear while you work, and sweep up sharp offcuts

practical2.title: Plan and organise a week's work for a fabrication team, and brief the team
practical2.brief: The assessor gives the group a set of four fabrication jobs with drawings or descriptions, estimated hours, due dates, the team's members and skills, one planned absence, the shared equipment and the current stock of key consumables. As a group: (1) sort the jobs by urgency and importance; (2) work out the team's capacity for the week and compare it with the hours needed; (3) draw a weekly schedule (bar chart or table) showing who does what each day; (4) book the shared equipment on a booking sheet; (5) check the consumables and work out what to order using the reorder point; and (6) write a short note to the supervisor on any shortfall and how to deal with it. Each member is responsible for one or two of these parts, using a spreadsheet or paper. Then one member gives a 5-minute briefing to the 'team' (the assessor and other members), and another answers a role-play call from a customer whose job will be late. Photograph each stage, including screens, and add them to the group's practical.
materials: The job pack from the assessor (jobs, hours, dates, team, absence, equipment, stock)
A computer with a spreadsheet, or squared paper, rulers and calculators
Booking sheet, order form and note templates
photos: The jobs sorted on an urgent–important grid
The stock check and order form
The customer call role play, with its notes
checklist: Took responsibility for their part and finished it
Sorted the jobs sensibly, with safety and deadlines first
Worked out capacity correctly, allowing for lost time and the absence
Schedule gives each person a fair, realistic load that matches their skills
Booked equipment without clashes and ordered stock using the reorder point
Raised the shortfall clearly with options
Briefed the team clearly or handled the customer call politely and honestly
Checked another member's work and helped correct it
safety: Plan the jobs with their hazards and PPE in mind, and show this in the schedule
Do not plan more than the Centre's rules allow for overtime or hours
Sit correctly at screens and take short breaks
Keep cables tidy and drinks away from computers
